title: The Seam Map
description: An 11-minute teaching explainer on the software development lifecycle as a chain of evidence, grounded in the COMP5241 lecture slides.

knowledgeNodes.title: The SDLC as a staged lifecycle
knowledgeNodes.summary: A structured lifecycle connects requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance, but the stages are not a one-way relay.

knowledgeNodes.title: Requirements: what vs how well
knowledgeNodes.summary: Functional requirements describe behavior; non-functional requirements describe operational quality. Both must become testable before they can be verified.

knowledgeNodes.title: Requirements come from people and evidence
knowledgeNodes.summary: Interviews, observation, documents, surveys, focus groups, and prototypes surface needs; clear questions and testable statements reduce ambiguity.

knowledgeNodes.title: Prototypes are learning instruments
knowledgeNodes.summary: Throwaway, evolutionary, and incremental prototypes answer different questions before full development.

knowledgeNodes.title: MVP is validated learning, not a smaller product
knowledgeNodes.summary: An MVP delivers enough core functionality to test whether customers will use the product, with the least effort.

knowledgeNodes.title: Design turns requirements into component responsibilities
knowledgeNodes.summary: Design describes how the system works: components, interfaces, data flow, trade-offs, and where risk is allocated.

knowledgeNodes.title: Secrets define a trust boundary
knowledgeNodes.summary: Local .env storage, .gitignore, and production environment-variable injection keep API keys out of the repository and frontend.

knowledgeNodes.title: Test levels move from units to seams to the system
knowledgeNodes.summary: Unit tests isolate components; integration tests expose interface mismatches; system tests check the whole requirement set.

knowledgeNodes.title: Build the product right vs build the right product
knowledgeNodes.summary: Verification checks conformance to specification; validation checks whether the product meets user and business needs.

knowledgeNodes.title: Validation feeds the next requirement
knowledgeNodes.summary: Validation produces new requirements, making the lifecycle a feedback loop rather than a relay.

knowledgeNodes.title: Production is a different environment
knowledgeNodes.summary: Development and production differ in libraries, data, access controls, limits, and external services, so local success is not production evidence.

knowledgeNodes.title: Maintenance is most of the lifecycle
knowledgeNodes.summary: Maintenance fixes, adapts, perfects, and prevents; it can average 60% of lifecycle cost and 60% of it is adding features while keeping the system running.

knowledgeNodes.title: The eighteen-hour visibility gap
knowledgeNodes.summary: The hypothetical incident runs from 1:00 AM deployment to 9:00 PM restoration; TTD, TTM, and TTR separate detection, mitigation, and customer impact.

knowledgeNodes.title: Availability and the cost of downtime
knowledgeNodes.summary: Availability is uptime divided by total time, described in 9s; the lecture relates it to MTTF and MTTR and gives downtime at several uptime levels.

knowledgeNodes.title: Deployment is a risk envelope
knowledgeNodes.summary: Big Bang, rolling, blue-green, and canary trade downtime, coexistence, rollback, and exposure to risk; feature flags separate release from deployment.

knowledgeNodes.title: From commit to monitored production
knowledgeNodes.summary: A CI/CD pipeline connects version control, build, test environments, staged rollout, and monitoring; it is the operational form of the lifecycle loop.

elements.content:
WHAT DID THE
LIFECYCLE MISS?
SCENARIO · PP. 41–42
A HYPOTHETICAL DEPLOYMENT
Health checks pass. No alarm fires. The incident has not officially started for the team.
A green check is a moment, not a trend.

narration.text: This is a hypothetical incident from the lecture. But the pattern is familiar.
At one a.m., the deployment is green. Health checks pass. The system looks stable.
Two hours later, the new queries begin to cascade. Response times fall, but no alarm fires.
At ten a.m., someone finally notices. The code passed every test. So what did the lifecycle miss?
A green check is a moment, not a trend. The first health check is a snapshot, not a guarantee.

elements.content:
NINE STAGES.
FOUR JOBS.
THE LIFECYCLE IS A CHAIN OF EVIDENCE
SHAPE → BUILD → PROVE → RUN · EACH STAGE LEAVES EVIDENCE

narration.text: The lecture lists nine stages: requirement analysis, system design, implementation, unit test, integration testing, system testing, acceptance testing, deployment, and maintenance.
Grouped, they do four jobs: shape the system, build it, prove it, and run it.
The important word is not stage. It is evidence.
A requirement retires value uncertainty. A design retires structural uncertainty. A test retires behavioural uncertainty.
Production retires the assumption that any of it survives contact with reality.
They are not a relay of completed documents. They are a chain of evidence, and the chain can break at any seam.

scenes.title: A requirement is a testable promise

elements.content:
A REQUIREMENT
IS A TESTABLE
PROMISE
WHAT VS HOW WELL

items.label: Functional — What it must accomplish: email, search, checkout
Non-functional — How well it operates: performance, reliability, security

elements.content: A confirmation email. An approval request. Search. A cart you can edit. Login. Notifications. Feedback.
“Easy to use” is a wish. “A new user completes checkout in under three minutes on a mid-range phone” is a requirement.
START WITH THE PROBLEM
PRIORITIZE · CONTROL CHANGE · VERIFY PURPOSE

narration.text: Functional requirements define what a system is supposed to accomplish.
Non-functional requirements define how well it operates: performance, reliability, usability, security.
The lecture's examples are ordinary: a confirmation email, an approval request, search, a cart you can edit, login, notifications, feedback.
None of these is a requirement until it is testable.
Easy to use is a wish. A new user can complete checkout in under three minutes on a mid-range phone is a requirement.
Start with the problem, not the solution. Then convert vague statements into testable, specific requirements or business rules.
If you cannot test it, it is not a requirement yet.

scenes.title: Ask the question behind the request

elements.content:
ASK THE
QUESTION
BEHIND THE
REQUEST
SIX WAYS TO SEE THE NEED
Documents show the official process. Observation shows the workaround. Interviews show the meaning. Surveys show the distribution. Focus groups show the conflict.
START WITH THE PROBLEM
MANAGE WHAT YOU LEARN: PRIORITIZE · CONTROL CHANGE · VERIFY PURPOSE

narration.text: Where do those requirements come from? The lecture lists six methods.
Document analysis, observation, interviews, surveys and questionnaires, focus groups, and prototyping.
Each method sees a different slice. Documents show the official process. Observation shows the workaround. Interviews show the meaning. Surveys show the distribution. Focus groups show the conflict.
Prototypes show what people actually do when they touch the thing.
A survey is not a conversation. An interview is not a sample. The best question is often, show me how you do it today.
Then manage what you learned: prioritize, control change, and verify that the system still meets its purpose.
The method is not the point. The question is.

elements.content:
PROTOTYPE BUYS
DESIGN LEARNING.
MVP BUYS
MARKET LEARNING.

elements.alt: MVP ladder: a partial car labeled not like this, and a skateboard-to-car progression labeled like this

elements.content: TWO DIFFERENT INSTRUMENTS

items.label: Prototype — Learn the design before full development
MVP — Learn the market with the least effort

elements.content: A prototype can be thrown away. An MVP cannot be fake: it must be usable enough to test demand.
MINIMUM ≠ SMALLEST

narration.text: A prototype is an umbrella term for an early deliverable built to show how requirements could be implemented.
Throwaway prototypes gather feedback and are discarded. Evolutionary prototypes are refined until the final version. Incremental prototypes build pieces separately.
An MVP is a different instrument. It is the smallest version that can collect the maximum validated learning about customers with the least effort.
Minimum means little effort. Viable means enough quality to test whether customers will use it.
The lecture's ladder makes the difference visible.

You do not build a car by shipping four wheels and a steering wheel. You build a skateboard, then a scooter, then a bicycle, then a car. Each step is usable, and each step teaches you something the next step needs.
The ladder is not about shipping less. It is about learning earlier.

scenes.title: Design is where risk gets a boundary

elements.content:
DESIGN IS WHERE
RISK GETS A
BOUNDARY

elements.alt: Source architecture: React frontend, Flask API backend, Azure OpenAI service, and chat history database

elements.content: FOUR RESPONSIBILITIES · THREE BOUNDARIES
Requirements say what. Design says how: components, interfaces, data flow, trade-offs.
EACH BOUNDARY IS A FAILURE POINT

narration.text: Requirements say what. Design says how: components, interfaces, data flow, trade-offs.
The lecture's example is a GenAI chat app.

A React frontend takes the student's question. A Python Flask API receives it, applies business logic, and calls an Azure OpenAI service. A database stores chat history. The answer travels back through the API to the student.
Four responsibilities, three boundaries.
Each boundary is a place where the system can fail: a malformed request, a slow model, a missing history record, a leaked key.
Good design is not a diagram with more boxes. It is a decision about where responsibility stops and where the next component begins.
The diagram is a claim about responsibility. That is why design is where risk gets a boundary.

elements.content:
THE SECRET
MUST NEVER
CROSS THE LINE

elements.alt: A .env file, a .gitignore shield, and a public GitHub repository with a lock

elements.content: A pushed key is already lost. Deleting the commit is not enough; rotate the key.
THREE RULES
ROTATE, DON’T JUST DELETE

narration.text: One boundary deserves its own minute: the secret.
The key lives in a local dot E N V file. Git ignore keeps that file out of version control. In production, the platform injects the key at deploy time.
The rule is absolute: secret keys and sensitive data must never appear in the remote repository.
Once a key is pushed, deleting the commit is not enough. You rotate the key.
The boundary is only real if the secret never crosses it.

elements.content:
UNIT, INTEGRATION,
SYSTEM, ACCEPTANCE

elements.alt: Input flows through Component 1 to Component 2 to Outcome, with a note that no bug is found in unit testing

elements.content: TEST A LARGER PROMISE AT EACH RUNG
Even a bug-free module can fail at the interface: Output 1 must equal Input 2. The seam is where two correct assumptions meet.

narration.text: Unit tests isolate a component. They answer a narrow question: does this function do what its design says?
Integration tests combine modules and test them as a group.

The lecture's example is precise: even when each module is correct and bug-free, a bug can appear when they are integrated. A calling module may misunderstand the interface specification of a called module.
System testing then checks the whole requirement set: functionality, robustness, interoperability, performance, scalability, reliability, documentation.
Acceptance testing hands the system to the customer or end user.
The pattern is a ladder: unit, integration, system, acceptance. Each rung tests a larger promise, and the seams are where the surprises live.
The seam is where two correct assumptions meet.

scenes.title: Build it right vs build the right thing

elements.content:
BUILD IT RIGHT.
BUILD THE RIGHT
THING.

elements.alt: Two panels: an engineer says the code is bug-free; a student asks whether it helps them learn

elements.content: TWO DIFFERENT QUESTIONS

items.label: Verification — Did we build the product right?
Validation — Did we build the right product?

elements.content: One asks whether the code conforms. The other asks whether it helps the student learn.
VALIDATION FEEDS THE NEXT REQUIREMENT

narration.text: Verification asks: did we build the product right?
Code review, unit testing, integration, system testing. It checks conformance to specification.
Validation asks: did we build the right product? Prototyping, acceptance testing, usability testing, testing in production, A B testing. It checks whether the product meets user and business needs.
The lecture's two-panel example is the whole argument. One engineer says, all systems go, the code is bug-free. The student says, but does it actually help my students learn?
Validation closes the loop. It leads to new requirements, and the lifecycle turns.
Verification without validation can produce a beautiful wrong product.

scenes.title: A release is a risk envelope

elements.content:
A RELEASE IS A
RISK ENVELOPE
Local green is not production evidence. OS, libraries, data, access, limits, and live services all differ.
FOUR WAYS TO EXPOSE RISK

items.label: Big Bang — One switch; downtime; rollback or outage
Rolling — Old and new coexist; replace gradually
Blue-Green — Two environments; switch traffic; switch back
Canary — Small user slice; widen only when clean

elements.content: RELEASE ≠ DEPLOY · FEATURE FLAGS
Same users, same load balancer. Only the blast radius changes.
Source diagrams: lecture pp. 52–55; credit @alexxubyte.

narration.text: Deployment is where the system meets an environment it does not control.
Development and production differ in OS versions, libraries, data, access controls, resource limits, and live services. Local green is not production evidence.
The lecture compares four strategies.
Big Bang rolls out the new version in one go, with downtime, and rolls back if it fails. It is risky for public-facing or business-critical applications.
Rolling upgrades replace the old version gradually. Old and new coexist, and incompatible components can be rolled back.
Blue-green keeps two identical production environments. Traffic moves from blue to green after testing, and can move back.
Canary routes a small portion of users to the new version first. With no errors, it gradually rolls out to the rest.
Feature flags separate release from deployment: visibility and activation can change without deploying new code.
The strategy chooses how much risk to expose, and to whom.

scenes.title: Maintenance is most of the lifecycle

elements.content:
MAINTENANCE IS
MOST OF THE
LIFECYCLE
SIXTY / SIXTY
FOUR KINDS OF MAINTENANCE
Maintenance happens on a running system, under time pressure, with incomplete information.
THE NEXT SECTION IS AN INCIDENT

narration.text: Maintenance is not the after-party.
The lecture reports that maintenance can average sixty percent of software lifecycle cost, and about sixty percent of maintenance is adding new features while keeping the system running.

The ISO standard gives four types: corrective, fixing defects; adaptive, remaining compatible with a changing environment; perfective, enhancing performance or maintainability; preventive, addressing potential issues before they become problems.
Maintenance happens on a running system, under time pressure, with incomplete information.
The system you maintain is never the system you designed.
That is why the next section is an incident.

elements.content:
THE CLOCK WAS
THE MISSING
SIGNAL

elements.alt: Timeline from 3:00 AM to 10:00 AM labeled The Visibility Gap, with waiting users and an operator asleep

elements.content: THE INCIDENT CLOCK
THREE CLOCKS + ONE BUDGET
HYPOTHETICAL SCENARIO
The system was down, but the incident had not officially started for the team. The signal that would have started the clock was missing.

narration.text: The incident began at three a.m. and was discovered at ten: seven hours of time to discover. No alarm fired.
The system was down, but the incident had not officially started for the team.
Diagnosis and repair took eight hours of time to mitigate. The queries lacked proper indexing, and they were locking resources.
The customer experienced eighteen hours of time to recover, from three a.m. to nine p.m.
These are different clocks. T T D measures observability. T T M measures operational velocity. T T R measures customer impact.
At four nines, the lecture's table allows about fifty two point five six minutes of downtime per year. At three nines, it is eight point seven six hours.
The clock makes the invisible cost visible.
The lifecycle did not fail because one test was missing. It failed because the signal that would have started the clock was missing.

scenes.title: The postmortem becomes the next requirement

elements.content:
NOT A RELAY.
A FEEDBACK
SYSTEM.
COMMIT → BUILD → TEST → RELEASE → MONITOR → LEARN
The postmortem is not the end of the incident. It is the next requirement.
MONITORING FEEDS THE NEXT REQUIREMENT
COMMIT → BUILD/TEST → QA/UAT → RELEASE → MONITOR

narration.text: The postmortem is not the end of the incident. It is the next requirement.
The big-tech pipeline in the lecture makes the loop concrete: commit, build and test, QA and UAT, release with feature toggles, canary and A B testing, then monitor.
Monitoring feeds the next requirement. The route line closes.
The S D L C is not a relay. It is a feedback system.
The loop is the only part that makes the lifecycle a system.
